header.deal: Pet-sitting app launching in Canada and the UK (company not named)
header.tag_why: The deal turned when a customer engineer used our docs and sandbox to build a working sitter payment flow over a weekend, after which the engineering decider 'stopped saying 'if''; marketplace onboarding and local-currency payouts were the supporting fit.

evidence.excerpt: Expansion. They were launching Canada, then the UK, and sitters have to get paid locally.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: a haunted house.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Two engineers more or less full-time just keeping sitter payments working.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: There was also a roadmap item, faster pay for sitters, that had been pushed three quarters in a row.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: Two pains came together. The expansion made local sitter pay mandatory, and the existing code was already eating engineers and blocking the faster-pay roadmap. The cost they felt was engineering capacity and a broken promise to sitters. It was not acceptance or global reach in the abstract, so our M1 opener speaks to the wrong pain.
trigger.messaging: For marketplace prospects, open on 'pay sitters locally in each new country without a team maintaining payments' (M11 plus M2), not on the generic M1 'every currency' line.

evidence.excerpt: Daniel. He signed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this is an engineering decision, finance will sign what I bring them.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: The CFO joined one call for ten minutes, asked one question
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: does this change when sitters get paid?
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: The VP of Engineering owned the decision outright. Finance asked only about the timing of sitter pay, which is the same 'paid by Friday' promise. Our ROI and economic-study message (M6) had no audience here. The transcript also never records what we told the CFO.
decider.messaging: In engineering-led deals, arm the VP Eng with build-time and maintenance-burden proof, and prepare one crisp line for finance on how sitter pay timing changes, or doesn't.

evidence.excerpt: I've stopped learning their names.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: A lot of pet owners pay with PayPal and Venmo, and they were nervous about what happens to those buttons.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Do we lose PayPal, do we lose Venmo, what happens to the saved cards.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I don't know that. That's me guessing.
evidence.label: opinion

competitor.insight: Mid-evaluation, the customer's questions moved from 'how fast can we build this' to 'what do we lose'. That loss framing is the real competitive threat, whoever planted it; the idea that Braintree did is the rep's admitted guess. It is also unclear whether the account-manager churn complaint was about Braintree or a separate current provider. That complaint is an opening, but our M5 tiered-response message doesn't speak to continuity of named people.
competitor.messaging: Build a 'what you keep' switching answer covering PayPal buttons, Venmo and saved cards, and use it before the customer asks, so the loss question never gets traction.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the docs and the sandbox.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And the marketplace piece. Onboarding sitters, the identity checks, paying out in local currency.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence: the acceptance-rate slide.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: M2 and M11 landed. M4 died on contact, because a low-ticket business that is drowning in maintenance doesn't rank auth-rate uplift as a problem. The rep delivered the full acceptance slide anyway and then moved on rather than reframing it. That slide was time not spent answering the PayPal and Venmo question that actually worried them.
message.messaging: Cut the auth-rate slide from low-ticket marketplace pitches and spend that time on a hands-on sandbox plus sitter onboarding and local pay.

evidence.excerpt: One of their engineers, on her own time, built a working sitter payment flow over a weekend and showed it at Monday standup.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: After that Daniel stopped saying 'if.'
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I didn't even know until Daniel told me.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Only that I barely sold this. Their engineer did.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The bake-off was settled by self-serve proof the customer produced on their own, and the rep was unaware of it at the time. That makes the win real but not repeatable as run. The rep's read that 'They decided it was a risk they'd take' on Venmo means we won despite open gaps, not because they were closed.
decided.messaging: Make 'build a working sitter pay flow in a weekend' an explicit, offered step in every engineering-led evaluation instead of hoping an engineer does it unprompted.

evidence.excerpt: Nothing, really. It was a clean one.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: I didn't have a crisp answer on Venmo in the room, and I still don't.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: who's done this at our size without losing cards?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we'll find out.
evidence.label: quote

gaps.insight: The rep called it 'a clean one', but three gaps remain open. Venmo has no answer, PayPal was deferred to implementation, and the same-size saved-card reference was promised and never sent. The customer raised saved cards again at kickoff, and the risk now sits with their engineers and our implementation. M8's 'customer stories' failed exactly when a specific peer reference was requested.
gaps.messaging: Get a referenceable saved-card migration story at a comparable size and a documented PayPal and Venmo answer. Until we have them, back 'nobody has to re-enter anything' with proof, not a doc and a conversation.

evidence.excerpt: We want to stop babysitting this.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: paid by Friday
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Nobody there says 'marketplace.' They say 'the app.'
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And nobody says 'payouts.' They say 'sitter pay.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: Their language is about engineering burden ('a haunted house', 'Payments shouldn't be a team') and a promise to sitters. Ours is category jargon: marketplace, payouts, authorization rates. Even the pitch that landed was framed in words they never use.
language.messaging: Rewrite M11 for this segment in their words, for example: get your sitters paid by Friday in every new country, and stop babysitting payments.

gaps.question: What did they ask for that we couldn't show?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya to list every open item from the evaluation (PayPal, Venmo, saved-card reference) and hand it to the implementation team now.

gaps.question: What is our answer on keeping Venmo?
gaps.follow_up: Ask product or solutions engineering for a definitive Venmo answer, and have Priya deliver it to Daniel.

gaps.question: Who has done a saved-card migration at their size without losing cards?
gaps.follow_up: Ask customer marketing or solutions for a comparable reference, and have Priya send it to Daniel, since it was promised and not delivered.

gaps.question: What did Braintree actually tell them?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Daniel or the engineer who built the prototype, in a win interview, what came out of the Braintree call.

gaps.question: Who was the incumbent provider, and was the account-manager churn theirs or Braintree's?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya who they were on before and whose account manager kept changing.

gaps.question: What did we answer to the CFO's question about when sitters get paid?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya what answer the CFO got, and whether faster sitter pay ('paid by Friday') is part of what was signed.

gaps.question: What does the signed deal cover: existing business, Canada, UK, or all of them?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya for the contracted scope and rollout order.

close.rep_takeaway: This deal was won by a sandbox you didn't know was being used. Next time, put it in the engineers' hands on purpose and stay close enough to see the moment it lands. Don't call a deal 'clean' while a promised reference and a Venmo answer are still open: closing those loops before signature is what keeps the kickoff from turning into 'we'll find out'.
